title: What If a DNA Test Said Your Kids Weren't Yours? In 2002 It Told a Mother

scenes.text: What if a DNA test said you weren't your own children's mother? In 2002, it happened.
A woman in Washington State applied for child support. Routine tests came back: no match, three times.
She was suspected of fraud. So when her third child was born, a court officer watched, and blood was drawn.
Two weeks later: still no match. To a baby they had seen her deliver.
Then doctors tested cells from her cervix. A second set of DNA, and it matched the children.
She was a chimera: two embryos, fraternal twins, had fused in the womb into one person. She is, in part, her own twin.

description:
What if a DNA test said you were not the mother of your own children? In 2002 it happened to a woman in Washington State when she applied for child support.
Three tests found no match and she was suspected of fraud; a court officer then witnessed the birth of her third child, and that test failed too. The answer was tetragametic chimerism: two fertilised eggs had fused early in the womb, so her body carried two cell lines. Her blood, skin and hair held one set of DNA and her cervix the other, which matched her children, and the case was dismissed. A similar case had been reported in the New England Journal of Medicine that same year. How common chimerism is remains unknown, because it can leave no outward sign.

first_comment: Neither woman in the two 2002 cases had any outward sign of it. How would you ever know? Drop your own what-if below.
